source.title: Mitigating Copy Bias in In-Context Learning through Neuron Pruning
source.authors: Ameen Ali; Lior Wolf; Ivan Titov

record.tranche_reason: The paper studies copying bias in ICL and pruning neurons associated with that bias. It does not measure induction heads, repeated-token induction, or their training dynamics, and does not rely on induction heads as a method or assumption.
record.gate_note: The paper cites work on induction heads in its related-work discussion, but its own copying-error definition concerns incorrect answers copied from example labels, not the [A][B] … [A] → [B] induction behaviour in the claim. The copying-error and ICL results below are related findings, not tests of the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The paper prunes MLP neurons tied to 'copying bias' (wrong answers copied from in-context labels) in pretrained LLMs. It never identifies induction heads or previous-token heads, never tracks training dynamics, and never measures loss against token index. Olsson et al. is cited only in related work. None of V1–V7 is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that pruning neurons linked to copying bias consistently improves few-shot ICL across tasks and architectures, including Mamba. They add that the pruned neurons appear to act as a shortcut that hinders task recognition, as shown by better task vectors.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Integrated Gradients on a synthetic vowel-counting task to identify and prune neurons associated with copying errors; it does not use the original induction-head identification or training-dynamics methods.
record.method_sensitivity: The pruning layer and percentage are selected using a proxy validation set; the procedure tests pruning rates from 1% to 10% in 1% increments.

fits_no_version.finding: Most errors on three few-shot ICL tasks are copying errors: wrong answers equal to a label in the prompt. Pruning IG-selected MLP neurons lowers copying errors and total errors in GPT2-Small, Bloom-560M and OPT-1.3B (figure only). Pruning also raises ICL accuracy across 18 tasks and improves task vectors.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Copying of in-context labels is a dominant error mode in few-shot ICL in small LLMs, driven partly by a sparse, task-agnostic set of MLP neurons whose pruning improves task recognition.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference of the European Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The copying-error results in Figure 2 are reported as plots without per-condition numerical values or uncertainty estimates. The paper does not measure induction-head behaviour or training-time formation.
record.rows_left_out: None from Figure 2. Other ICL accuracy and task-vector results are not separately cataloged here because they measure task performance or task-vector accuracy rather than the copying-error outcome shown in these rows; neither bears on an induction-head version.

untested.parts: Induction-head and previous-token-head composition and the [A][B]…[A]→[B] circuit are not examined.
No training-time analysis of when heads form, of ICL gains, or of a loss bump.
No measure of induction heads' share of in-context learning (loss falling with token index).
Induction heads are not detected in any of the models tested (GPT2, Bloom, OPT, Llama, Mamba).
No manipulation of training data or setup.
Few-shot task accuracy and task vectors are measured, but no head-level attribution separates induction heads from other mechanisms.
No analysis of how formation unfolds over training.

record.verdict_notes: The record's gate is correct: 'copying bias' here means label copying in pretrained models, studied at MLP-neuron level. It is not induction-head behaviour. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The fits_no_version entry is kept and broadened to cover the accuracy and task-vector results.

versions.untested_parts: Whether induction heads compose with previous-token heads or implement the stated repeated-token copying circuit.
Whether induction heads form abruptly during training or coincide with an ICL gain and a loss-curve bump.
Whether induction heads carry most ICL in large transformers.
Whether induction heads occur across model families, sizes, training runs, architectures, or modalities.
Whether data or training setup changes induction-head formation or the persistence of ICL.
Whether few-shot task learning runs mainly through mechanisms other than induction heads.
Whether induction-head formation consists of multiple sub-steps or overlapping transitions.
